stories.title: 'He saved my life': Hometown veteran meets man who saved his life through bone marrow donation
stories.summary: A Marine Corps veteran battling cancer finally met the stranger who saved his life: a bone marrow donor who signed up a decade ago. Turns out, they live just miles apart in Wisconsin.
stories.extended_summary: Henry Douglas was two steps from death when he arrived at the hospital. The Marine Corps veteran had been fighting cancer and needed a stem cell transplant to survive. Enter Ethan Massen, who had signed up for the bone marrow registry 10 years earlier and didn't hesitate when he got the call that he was a match. On November 11, the two met face-to-face for the first time at Aurora St. Luke's in Milwaukee. 'I wanted to shake the hand of the man who prolonged my life,' Douglas said. 'He saved my life.' The kicker? Donors and recipients rarely live in the same state—but these two discovered they're practically neighbors.

stories.summary: After a sniper's bullet left him paralyzed in Iraq, Marine veteran Mike Delancey turned his recovery into a mission. What started as a way to keep fellow wounded warriors active has become a global adaptive sports powerhouse in Tampa Bay.
stories.extended_summary: Mike Delancey was patrolling in Iraq when a sniper's bullet nearly ended his life. He was unconscious for six weeks while doctors in Germany told his father to prepare to say goodbye. He survived but lost the use of his legs. Rather than retreat, Delancey and his father opened the Wounded Warriors Abilities Ranch in Pinellas Park in 2015—a space for injured veterans to stay active and connected. Now, every Tuesday and Thursday, the Lealman Exchange Center hums with adaptive athletes training for championships. What began as a local effort to keep veterans moving has grown into an internationally recognized adaptive sports empire, all rooted in one Marine's refusal to give up.

stories.extended_summary: Sherrie James was doing her hair when she heard a crash. Her grandson yelled, 'You've got a hole in your ceiling!' A meteorite—roughly the size of a large fist—had torn through the roof, smashed into her daughter's bedroom floor, bounced to the ceiling, and landed by the bed. It was a chunk of an asteroid formed 4.5 billion years ago, part of a meteor that NASA estimates weighed a ton and broke apart over Texas at 35,000 mph. For James, it was a defining moment that brought existential questions about her place in the universe literally into her home. She decided to give it to the Houston Museum of Natural Science, where it can be studied and shared.

'This was a moment we will truly never forget,' they said. 'A once-in-a-lifetime experience.'

stories.title: Bay Area boy celebrates year in remission after rare blood cancer diagnosis
stories.summary: Lennox Pieraldi was 8 months old when doctors found three tumors in his head — a rare blood cancer called LCH. After chemo stopped working, a 12-month clinical trial at UCSF changed everything. Now 3, he's celebrating a year in remission.
stories.extended_summary: It started with a little bump on his gums. Doctors eventually found three tumors in Lennox Pieraldi's head — one in his gums, one behind his eye, another near the base of his brain. He was just 8 months old, diagnosed with Langerhans cell histiocytosis, a rare blood cancer. Chemotherapy and steroids worked for about a year, then stopped.
